what_it_does: Quantum computers use fragile quantum bits (qubits) whose states must be read out quickly and accurately — a process called qubit readout. Current neural-network-based readout systems are large and slow, and they cannot support mid-circuit measurements (reading a qubit partway through a computation without disturbing the rest), which are essential for quantum error correction. KLiNQ uses a teacher–student technique called knowledge distillation, where a large, accurate neural network teaches a tiny student network to mimic its behavior, shrinking model size by 99% while keeping 91% accuracy. Each qubit gets its own dedicated tiny network running on a field-programmable gate array (an FPGA — a chip whose internal logic circuits can be reconfigured after manufacture), completing each readout in just 32 nanoseconds. This approach is based on the abstract only, so details of the training process and real-world error correction integration are uncertain.
